where: Executive summary #8 — The product that people loved is fully documented and still buildable
claim: Strip out the monetisation story and the corpus is an unusually clean specification for a habit tracker people were delighted by: minimal (27.45%), beautiful (13.27%), unlimited, ad-free, and — the genuine differentiator — a non-streak 'habit strength' percentage that decays instead of resetting (0.94% explicit praise, the highest-affection language in the corpus); that decay model was itself broken by the 2021 rewrite and never restored
this_app_does: minimal, beautiful, unlimited, ad-free, decaying strength %

where: §3.4 The forgiving habit-strength model — the real differentiator
claim: A non-streak habit-strength percentage that decays instead of resetting — missing a day reduces the score instead of zeroing a streak, which prevents the 'what the hell' abandonment spiral: 'most focus too much on streaks… missing one day and breaking my streak tends to send me into a spiral where I give up'; a DE user explains it as logarithmic rather than linear and 'much closer to psychological reality'; the decay behaviour broke in the 2021 rewrite and was never restored
this_app_does: decaying strength % instead of streaks; broken 2021
magnitude: 38 explicit (0.94%), mean 3.95 — highest-affection language in the corpus

where: §3.5 Misunderstandings — the habit-strength percentage is a documentation failure, not a maths failure
claim: Users cannot work out what the strength number means — a weekly habit completed once shows 4%, not 100%; the developer's answer that it takes ~91 repetitions to reach 100% reads as arbitrary; a documentation failure, not a maths failure, and the one complaint that is cheap to fix

A one-screen explainer — 'a weekly habit completed once shows 4% because the score measures strength over ~91 repetitions, not this week's completion' — plus an optional 'this period' toggle; the cheapest satisfaction win available

where: Part 0 §7 (What actually makes people love this app: the GitHub grid, and doing nothing else)
claim: Three tightly coupled praise clusters describe one product decision — the GitHub grid and doing nothing else: simplicity / no bloat, design / visual appeal, and the grid heat-map itself, which reviewers spontaneously call 'GitHub', 'contribution graph', 'commits', 'Seinfeld / don't break the chain'
Week / month / year grid views are the emotional payoff — 'filling the squares' is the retention mechanic
Cumulative totals ('how many total hours have I spent on this habit?') are requested, not just streaks
A total-days counter instead of consecutive-days, to reduce streak anxiety
side_effects: streak anxiety is a churn mechanism the report takes seriously despite n=1

claim: People value a simple, free counter that makes breaking a streak feel costly: U:praise_any 476 (77.52%, CI 74.1–80.6%, 4.81★), U:praise_specific 285 (46.42%) (verbatim): Code / union | n | % of 614 | What it records ; PRAISE_SIMPLE_EASY | 132 | 21.50% | simple, "nothing extra", convenient, intuitive ; U:outcome_any | 118 | 19.22% | the app helped them quit, abstain, or stay motivated ; U:tracking_core_praise | 72 | 11.73% | the counter, several habits at once, or the relapse notes ; U:free_or_ads_praise | 43 | 7.00% | free, no subscription, no or few ads ; PRAISE_DESIGN | 39 | 6.35% | minimal, beautiful, non-triggering design ; PRAISE_GENERIC | 184 | 29.97% | approval with no named quality — the mechanism is the number itself: 'breaking big numbers hurts far more than the urge to smoke' (ru, 4★); 'one reason not to relapse was that all the days would reset' (by, a month without cigarettes); 'seeing the numbers clearly calms me more than a pile of praise'; minimalism is a feature for this audience — 'the interface doesn't trigger — important for people with addictions, where an extra detail can set you off'; counter, reset and a diary-like comment 'to analyse a slip. Nothing else is needed'; free with many habits at once is what switchers name — 'the only free app so far that allows this without a subscription' (de); 'not forcing ads or payments like every other app, only free one out there' (us).
this_app_does: counter to the second + reset + relapse note; nothing else
magnitude: praise_any 476 / 77.52% / 4.81★; SIMPLE_EASY 132 / 21.50%; outcome_any 118 / 19.22%; tracking_core 72; free_or_ads 43; DESIGN 39; GENERIC 184
conditions: the loss-aversion of a big number is the retention mechanic — the app needs no gamification beyond the count

claim: For a meaningful minority this is a recovery tool for self-harm and drugs: U:safety_sensitive 23 (3.75%, CI 2.5–5.6%, 4.96★) — USE_SELF_HARM 13 (2.12%), USE_DRUGS 8 (1.30%), USE_TREATMENT_CONTEXT 3; 'with this app I haven't harmed myself for a month'; self-harming for a year — 'this app really helps me hold back' (kz); 'held on almost a week, tracking in the app, but couldn't' (us); 'stopped snorting cocaine' (by, 7 votes); 'two rehabs didn't help'; a relapse log kept for a psychiatrist ('it's easier for my psychiatrist'); the listing describes smoking, alcohol, gambling and nail-biting and does not mention self-harm — 'the app is already used for self-harm recovery by reviewers who are likely young; its content, relapse copy and any ads shown to them are a safety question'.

where: §3.3.4 The expensive failure — a paying user never used the product because skip / miss / stat semantics were opaque ('what does it mean when you forget to record a habit as completed, is that skipped or recorded as a miss. I don't understand how the stats work'); same gap five years later ('you don't understand whether you forgot to tick that day or whether it was a skip')
claim: Make skip vs miss vs not-logged visibly distinct and explain the stats: a paying user never used the app because the semantics were opaque — 'what does it mean when you forget to record a habit as completed, is that skipped or recorded as a miss. I don't understand how the stats work' (GB, 3★); five years later the same question — 'when you go into a habit's history and see gaps, you don't understand whether you forgot to tick that day or whether it was a skip. It's somehow not obvious' (UA, 4★)

Make skip / miss / not-yet visually distinct in history — five years apart, same ambiguity, and it cost one payer the entire value of the purchase; a distinct 'not achieved' (未達) state and a 'mark no if you missed it' option are asked for

Milestone celebration / badges (235, 2.21%, mean 4.74) is the largest positive-intent feature request in the corpus, spanning 2020→2026 in every era — almost all 4–5★ users describing a gap; Achievements shipped in v4.1.0 (31 Aug 2026), post-dating almost all of them
conditions: a six-year-old top request; whether it becomes a purchase driver is not yet visible

claim: Milestone celebration and achievements — 235 requests over six years; v4.1.0 appears to address this, validate against the 3–4★ band in the next corpus
